mainTopic: When does an object count as 'resting' (הנחה) for the laws of carrying on שבת? רבא's explanations: the inclined wall, water on top of water, and the nut floating in a vessel.
overview: This עמוד asks when an object counts as having 'come to rest' (הנחה) for the laws of carrying on שבת. First the גמרא recalls a משנה about a scroll that rolled off a roof. רבא explains that the scroll lies on a slanted wall (כותל משופע), so it counts as resting. That answer does not work for flowing water. So רבא explains that the water was scooped from a hole already full of water, because water on top of water counts as resting. A nut floating on water does not count as resting. רבא's question about a nut inside a floating vessel stays a doubt (תיקו). Oil floating on wine is tied to a dispute between רבי יוחנן בן נורי and the רבנן. Next, רבי יוחנן rules that a loaded person who wanders in and out is not liable until he stops, and אביי adds that the stop must be to rest. Finally, a ברייתא about carrying from a store to a plaza through a colonnade raises the question of liability through a middle domain, and רבי יוחנן's answer begins at the end of the עמוד and continues on the next one.

steps.title: The משנה of the scroll that rolled away
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה: if a scroll rolls from a threshold, he may roll it back. If it rolls off a roof, he may roll it back only until it comes within ten טפחים of the ground. After that, he only turns it face-down.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone was reading a scroll on a threshold and it rolled out of his hand, he may roll it back to himself. If he was reading on top of a roof and the scroll rolled out of his hand, he may roll it back as long as it has not reached within ten handbreadths of the ground. Once it has reached within ten handbreadths, he turns it over onto its writing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting a משנה about a scroll that rolled away on שבת. This sets up the next move: the גמרא will ask a question about this משנה and bring רבא's answer, to see whether it can help with the water case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: While the scroll is still high up, more than ten טפחים above the ground, it has not entered the public area, so he may pull it back. Once it hangs within ten טפחים of the public ground, it is treated as being in רשות הרבים. Pulling it back would then be carrying, so he may only turn it face-down to protect the holy writing.

keyTerms.meaning: He rolls it back to himself
Ten handbreadths, the height that separates the public domain from the air above it
He turns it over onto its writing (face-down)

steps.confusionAlert: Turning the scroll face-down is not about carrying at all. It is only about protecting the dignity of the holy writing, because he is not allowed to bring the scroll back.

phrases.english: If one was reading a scroll on the threshold
and the scroll rolled from his hand
he may roll it back to himself.
phrases.notes: One end is still in his hand.

phrases.english: If he was reading on top of the roof
and the scroll rolled from his hand,
as long as it has not reached within ten handbreadths (of the ground)
he may roll it back to himself.
Once it has reached within ten handbreadths
he turns it over onto its writing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings an outside משנה as a parallel for the earlier question about flowing water.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Within ten טפחים of public ground, the scroll may not be pulled back; he only turns it face-down.

steps.title: But the scroll never came to rest
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא recalls that it once challenged this משנה: why can't he pull the scroll back, if it never landed and rested anywhere?
steps.simpleTranslation: And we discussed this: why must he turn it over onto its writing? It has not come to rest!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא remembers a challenge it once raised on this משנה. A dangling scroll never actually landed anywhere, so why is pulling it back forbidden?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Carrying on שבת requires lifting an object from a place where it rests and putting it down. A scroll that only hangs in the air within ten טפחים has not 'rested' in רשות הרבים. So pulling it back should not count as lifting it from there.

keyTerms.meaning: And we discussed / raised a difficulty on it
But it has not come to rest!

phrases.english: And we discussed it:
Why must he turn it over onto its writing?
It has not come to rest!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָוֵינַן בַּהּ: אַמַּאי הוֹפְכוֹ עַל הַכְּתָב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of the משנה just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that he may not pull back the scroll once it is within ten טפחים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An object that never rested in רשות הרבים cannot be 'lifted' from there, so pulling it back should be allowed.

steps.title: רבא: the scroll rests on a slanted wall
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the case is a slanted wall. The scroll lies on the wall, so it counts as having come to rest.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא said: it is referring to an inclined wall.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the challenge. The scroll fell against a slanted wall, so it is lying on something and counts as resting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A slanted wall gives the scroll a surface to lean on, so it has a real 'resting place' within ten טפחים. That is why pulling it back is forbidden. The גמרא brought this answer hoping to apply the same idea to water flowing down a wall.

phrases.english: And Rava said:
It refers to an inclined wall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The scroll is hanging in the air and never rested.
steps.terutzMaskana: The scroll is lying on a slanted wall, which counts as a resting place.

steps.title: Water does not rest on a slanted wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects using רבא's slanted-wall answer for the water case. A scroll stays put on a slanted wall, but water keeps running down.
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted that רבא said this about a scroll, which tends to rest there. But does water tend to rest?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back: the slanted-wall idea works for a scroll but not for water. So the water case needs a different explanation, which the next step gives.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A scroll can lie still on a slanted wall. Water on a slanted wall keeps flowing and never stops anywhere. So the water case still lacks a real 'resting place.'

phrases.english: Granted that Rava said this regarding a scroll,
which tends to come to rest;
but does water tend to come to rest?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects applying step 3's answer to the water case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the use of the slanted-wall answer for water. רבא's answer about the scroll still stands.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Water flows and cannot rest on a slanted surface, unlike a scroll.

steps.title: רבא's new answer: scooped from a hole
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives a new explanation of the water case. The person gathered the water from on top of a hole (גומא) full of water.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: the case is where he gathered the water from on top of a hole.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the slanted wall does not work for water, רבא offers a different setup. The water had collected in a hole, and he took it from there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Water that pooled in a hole has stopped flowing and is sitting in place. Taking it from there is lifting it from a resting place, so he is liable.

keyTerms.meaning: A hole or pit in the ground

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
For example, where he gathered it from on top of a hole.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא: כְּגוֹן שֶׁקָּלַט מֵעַל גַּבֵּי גּוּמָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected slanted-wall answer with a new case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The water was flowing down a wall and never rested.
steps.terutzMaskana: The water was taken from a hole where it had pooled, which counts as resting.

steps.title: A hole is obvious
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: if the water was in a hole, of course it was resting. Why would anyone need to teach that?
steps.simpleTranslation: A hole? That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's new answer as too obvious to be the point of the teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Water sitting in a hole is clearly at rest, so the ruling seems to teach nothing new. The גמרא expects every teaching to add something.

phrases.english: A hole? That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 5 as obvious.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's case of water taken from a hole
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Water in a hole is clearly resting, so the teaching adds nothing.

steps.title: The new point: water on water counts as resting
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that it is not obvious. One might think water landing on other water has not really 'rested,' so the teaching says that it has.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said that water on top of water is not considered resting. So he teaches us that it is.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what is new in רבא's answer. The rain fell into a hole that already held water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Water landing on other water has no solid surface under it, so one might think it is not resting. רבא teaches that the water below counts as its resting place. This is the real new point.

keyTerms.meaning: Placement / resting (one of the two parts of carrying)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a key rule for the laws of carrying: a liquid can 'rest' on another liquid.

phrases.english: You might have said

phrases.aramaic: מַיִם עַל גַּבֵּי מַיִם לָאו הַנָּחָה הוּא,
phrases.english: that water on top of water is not considered resting;
so he teaches us (that it is).

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא מַיִם עַל גַּבֵּי מַיִם לָאו הַנָּחָה הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge of step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifying the חידוש (the new point being taught)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Water resting on water is not a real resting.
steps.terutzMaskana: Water on water does count as הנחה.

steps.title: רבא is consistent: water on water vs. a nut on water
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that רבא follows his own rule stated elsewhere. Water on water counts as resting, but a nut floating on water does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא follows his own reasoning, for רבא said: water on top of water is its resting place. A nut on top of water is not its resting place.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רבא's answer matches another rule of his. Along the way it adds a contrasting case: a floating nut.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Water blends into the water below, so it is truly resting there. A nut bobs and drifts on the surface and is not settled. So lifting a nut off water is not lifting from a resting place.

phrases.english: And Rava follows his own reasoning,
for Rava said:

phrases.aramaic: מַיִם עַל גַּבֵּי מַיִם — הַיְינוּ הַנָּחָתָן.
phrases.english: Water on top of water: that is its resting place.

phrases.aramaic: אֱגוֹז עַל גַּבֵּי מַיִם — לָאו הַיְינוּ הַנָּחָתוֹ.
phrases.english: A nut on top of water: that is not its resting place.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 7 by pointing to רבא's own rule elsewhere.
steps.raayaObject: That רבא holds water on water counts as הנחה
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבא's independent statement about water on water and a nut on water

steps.title: רבא's question: a nut in a floating vessel
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks about a nut lying inside a vessel that floats on water. Do we look at the nut, which sits still in the vessel, or at the vessel, which drifts?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: a nut in a vessel, and the vessel floats on water. Do we go after the nut, and it is resting? Or perhaps we go after the vessel, and it is not resting, because it moves.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא raises a new, harder case between his two rules. It asks which object decides whether there is a resting place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The nut itself is still inside the vessel, so it seems to be resting. But the vessel under it drifts on the water, just like a floating nut. The question is whether we judge by the item itself or by what holds it.

phrases.english: Rava asked:

phrases.aramaic: אֱגוֹז בִּכְלִי וּכְלִי צָף עַל גַּבֵּי מַיִם,
phrases.english: A nut in a vessel, and the vessel floats on water:
do we go after the nut, and it is resting?
Or perhaps we go after the vessel,
and it is not resting, since it moves.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רָבָא: אֱגוֹז בִּכְלִי וּכְלִי צָף עַל גַּבֵּי מַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends step 8's rules to a mixed case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether resting is judged by the object itself (the nut) or by its container (the floating vessel).

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The question is left open: תיקו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand (unresolved).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the discussion without answering רבא's question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source settles whether we judge by the nut or by the vessel. So the case remains a doubt.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand: the question remains unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: Water on water counts as resting (הנחה). A nut floating on water does not. A nut inside a floating vessel is an unresolved doubt (תיקו).

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes רבא's question without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The case of a nut in a floating vessel remains unresolved.

steps.title: Oil floating on wine depends on a dispute
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a similar case of oil floating on wine. It says the answer depends on a dispute between רבי יוחנן בן נורי and the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Oil floating on top of wine: this is the dispute of רבי יוחנן בן נורי and the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from the floating nut to a similar case: oil floating on wine. It says this case depends on an existing dispute. The next step will show that dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Oil does not mix with wine. It sits on top as a separate layer. If the oil counts as connected to the wine, it is like water on water and counts as resting. If it counts as separate, it is like a nut floating on water and does not count as resting.

phrases.english: Oil that floats on top of wine,

phrases.aramaic: מַחֲלוֹקֶת רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן נוּרִי וְרַבָּנַן.
phrases.english: is the dispute of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and the Rabbis.
phrases.notes: The question is whether the oil counts as part of the wine.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁמֶן שֶׁצָּף עַל גַּבֵּי יַיִן, מַחֲלוֹקֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the nut question ends in תיקו, the גמרא raises a similar floating case and ties it to a known dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whether oil on wine counts as resting depends on the dispute between רבי יוחנן בן נורי and the רבנן.

steps.title: The משנה about a טבול יום touching oil on wine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה. A טבול יום who touches the oil makes only the oil impure, according to the רבנן. רבי יוחנן בן נורי says both are connected.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned: Oil floating on wine, and a טבול יום touched the oil: he disqualifies only the oil. רבי יוחנן בן נורי says: the two are connected to each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows where the dispute from the last step comes from. It is a משנה about impurity.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן treat the oil as a separate thing, so only the oil becomes disqualified. רבי יוחנן בן נורי treats oil and wine as one connected unit, so both become disqualified. The same question, connected or separate, decides whether oil on wine counts as resting for שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: as we learned in a משנה
someone who immersed today but must wait for nightfall to be fully pure

steps.confusionAlert: This משנה is about טומאה, not about שבת. The גמרא uses it only because it shows whether oil and wine are seen as one connected unit.

phrases.aramaic: דִּתְנַן: שֶׁמֶן שֶׁצָּף עַל גַּבֵּי יַיִן
phrases.english: As we learned: oil floating on top of wine
and one who immersed that day touched the oil —
he disqualified only the oil alone.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says:
The two of them are connected to each other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides the source for the dispute mentioned in step 11.
steps.raayaObject: That oil on wine depends on whether the two are connected.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in טבול יום: the רבנן say only the oil is disqualified, and רבי יוחנן בן נורי says both are.
steps.whatToRemember: Oil on wine: the רבנן see it as separate, so it is like the nut. רבי יוחנן בן נורי sees it as connected, so it is like water on water.

steps.title: Walking in and out all day while loaded is not liable until he stops
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן rules that a person loaded with food and drink who goes in and out of domains all day is not liable until he stops.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבין said in the name of רבי אילעאי in the name of רבי יוחנן: If someone was loaded with food and drinks and went in and out all day long, he is not liable until he stands still.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new rule from רבי יוחנן. Someone picked up food planning to move it only within one domain, then changed his mind and kept walking in and out of domains.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To be liable for carrying out, the lifting (עקירה) has to be done for the purpose of carrying out. This person lifted the load for a different purpose, so all his walking does not count. Only once he stops does the load count as put down. When he starts walking again, that is a new, proper lift.

keyTerms.meaning: goes in and goes out (between domains)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אָבִין אָמַר רַבִּי אִילְעַאי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Avin said that Rabbi Ilai said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
If he was loaded with food and drinks,
and he went in and out the whole day long —
he is not liable until he stands still.
phrases.notes: Stopping counts as putting the load down. Walking again afterward is a proper new lift.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אָבִין אָמַר רַבִּי אִילְעַאי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic: the person's own body carrying the load, and the need for a proper עקירה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person who wanders in and out with a load he did not lift in order to carry out is not liable until he stops.

steps.title: אביי: only stopping to rest counts
steps.stepSummary: אביי adds a limit. The stop counts only if he stopped to rest.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: And this is only when he stopped to rest.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי narrows רבי יוחנן's rule. Not every stop counts, only a stop to rest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he stops just to fix the load on his shoulder, that is part of carrying, not a putting-down. Only a real rest counts as placing the load. So only after a resting stop does his next walk begin a new, proper lift.

keyTerms.meaning: and this is only when (a limiting phrase)

phrases.english: Abaye said:
And that is when he stopped to rest.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines which kind of stop in רבי יוחנן's rule counts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only stopping to rest counts as placing the load. Stopping to adjust it does not.

steps.title: Proof from the ברייתא about stopping within four אמות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where אביי learned this. It answers from a teaching about stopping within four אמות and beyond four אמות.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where? From what the master said: Within four אמות, if he stopped to rest, he is exempt; if he stopped to adjust his load, he is liable. Beyond four אמות, if he stopped to rest, he is liable; if he stopped to adjust his load, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for אביי's source and brings it. The source is a teaching about carrying in the public domain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Stopping to rest counts as putting the load down. So if he rests before four אמות, he never carried four full אמות and is exempt. If he rests after four אמות, he has finished the act and is liable. Stopping to adjust does not count as putting down, so the results are reversed. This shows that only resting is a placing.

keyTerms.meaning: four cubits, the distance for liability in the public domain
to adjust the load on the shoulder

steps.confusionAlert: The rulings flip between 'within' and 'beyond' four אמות. Resting means the act is finished at that spot. Adjusting means the act is not finished yet. Track that one idea and the flip makes sense.

phrases.english: From where? From what the master said:

phrases.aramaic: תּוֹךְ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת עָמַד לָפוּשׁ — פָּטוּר,
phrases.english: Within four cubits, if he stopped to rest, he is exempt,
if he stopped to adjust the load, he is liable.

phrases.aramaic: חוּץ לְאַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת, עָמַד לָפוּשׁ — חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: Beyond four cubits, if he stopped to rest, he is liable.
If he stopped to adjust the load, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for אביי's limit.
steps.raayaObject: That only stopping to rest counts as placing the load.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A teaching that stopping to rest ends the carrying act and stopping to adjust does not, both within and beyond four אמות.

steps.title: Why did רבי יוחנן need to say this again?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רבי יוחנן's rule adds. He already taught the same idea in the case of moving objects from corner to corner.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is he teaching us? That the first lift was not for this purpose? רבי יוחנן already said that once! As רב ספרא said in the name of רבי אמי in the name of רבי יוחנן: Someone who moves objects from corner to corner, then changes his mind and takes them out, is exempt, because the first lift was not for that purpose.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן's teaching as repetitive. He already taught the same principle in another case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea behind both rulings is the same: the lift must be done for the purpose of carrying out. In the corner-to-corner case he already taught that changing your mind in the middle does not make you liable. So why teach it again with the loaded person?

keyTerms.meaning: lifting an object from its place, the start of carrying

phrases.english: What is he teaching us?

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא הָיְתָה עֲקִירָה מִשָּׁעָה רִאשׁוֹנָה לְכָךְ?
phrases.english: That the lifting from the first moment was not for this purpose?

phrases.aramaic: הָא אַמְרַהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן חֲדָא זִימְנָא!
phrases.english: But Rabbi Yochanan already said it once!

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב סָפְרָא אָמַר רַבִּי אַמֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: As Rav Safra said that Rabbi Ami said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
One who moves objects from corner to corner,
and changed his mind about them and took them out, is exempt,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא הָיְתָה עֲקִירָה מִשָּׁעָה רִאשׁוֹנָה לְכָךְ.
phrases.english: because the lifting from the first moment was not for this purpose.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to רבי יוחנן's rule itself and questions why it was needed.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's rule about the loaded person going in and out.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same principle, that a lift not meant for carrying out does not make one liable, was already taught by רבי יוחנן in the corner-to-corner case, so this would be a repeat.

steps.title: Two students reported one teaching in two ways
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי יוחנן taught the idea only once. Two אמוראים reported it, each using a different case.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are different אמוראים. One master said it in this wording, and the other master said it in that wording.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. רבי יוחנן did not repeat himself. Two different reporters passed on his one teaching in two different forms.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אילעאי reported it as the loaded person going in and out. רבי אמי reported it as the corner-to-corner case. It is one principle, so nothing is repeated.

keyTerms.meaning: master, a respectful way to refer to a Sage

steps.whatToRemember: A lift must be made in order to carry out. Changing your mind midway does not make you liable until you truly stop to rest and lift again. רבי יוחנן taught this once, and two reporters passed it on with different cases.

phrases.english: They are different amoraim,
one master said it in this wording,
and the other master said it in that wording.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge that רבי יוחנן repeated himself.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different transmitters of a single statement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן said the same rule twice, which seems unnecessary.
steps.terutzMaskana: He said it only once. רבי אילעאי and רבי אמי each reported it using a different case.

steps.title: Carrying from a store to a plaza through a colonnade
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that someone who carries from a store to a plaza by way of a colonnade is liable. בן עזאי says he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: One who carries something out of a store into a plaza, passing through a colonnade on the way, is liable. בן עזאי says he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about a person who carries from a private area to a public area but walks through an in-between area on the way. The רבנן and בן עזאי disagree about whether he is liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The store is a רשות היחיד and the plaza is a רשות הרבים. The colonnade in between is a כרמלית, an area that the Torah does not treat as either one. The question is whether passing through that middle area breaks the act of carrying into two separate pieces.

keyTerms.meaning: "The Rabbis taught": this introduces a ברייתא
A store, which counts as a private domain (רשות היחיד)
A plaza or open square, which counts as a public domain (רשות הרבים)
A colonnade or porch between the store and the street. It has the status of a כרמלית
Exempts. He holds the person is not liable

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the person put the object down in the colonnade. He only walked through it while holding the object. The whole argument is about walking through, not resting the object there.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who carries out from a store to a plaza
phrases.notes: From a private domain to a public domain.

phrases.english: by way of a colonnade is liable.
phrases.notes: The colonnade is a כרמלית in between.

phrases.english: And Ben Azzai exempts him.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַמּוֹצִיא מֵחֲנוּת לִפְלַטְיָא דֶּרֶךְ סְטָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After discussing stopping and resting during הוצאה, the גמרא moves to a related, harder case: carrying through an in-between domain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The רבנן hold that carrying from a store to a plaza through a colonnade makes one liable. בן עזאי holds that one is exempt.

steps.title: בן עזאי makes sense, but where do we find the רבנן's kind of liability?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains בן עזאי's reasoning: walking is like standing. It then challenges the רבנן: where do we find someone liable in a case like this?
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for בן עזאי: he holds that walking is like standing still. But the רבנן, even if they hold that walking is not like standing, where do we ever find someone liable in a case like this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא first explains why בן עזאי exempts the person. Then it challenges the רבנן, asking where we find liability when the object did not go straight from one domain to the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For בן עזאי, every step counts as stopping, so the person 'stopped' in the כרמלית. That means he never carried straight from רשות היחיד to רשות הרבים. The רבנן reject this idea, but the problem remains: the object still passed through a כרמלית, and the גמרא asks where we find liability for carrying by way of a middle domain.

keyTerms.meaning: "Granted" or "it makes sense": admits one side before challenging the other
Walking is considered like standing still
"Even if we grant": accepts a point but shows the problem remains
"Where do we find?": asks for a precedent

steps.confusionAlert: The question against the רבנן does not depend on the walking-standing debate. Even after we accept that walking is not standing, the object still crossed through a middle domain. The question is where the Torah makes someone liable for that.

phrases.english: Granted, Ben Azzai,
he holds that walking is like standing.
phrases.notes: So each step counts as a stop in the colonnade.

phrases.english: But the Rabbis,
even granting that they hold
that walking is not like standing,
where do we find a case like this where one is liable?
phrases.notes: He wants another case where someone is liable even though the item passed through an in-between area.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא בֶּן עַזַּאי, קָסָבַר מְהַלֵּךְ כְּעוֹמֵד דָּמֵי. אֶלָּא רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains one side of the ברייתא and challenges the other side.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view of the רבנן in the ברייתא, that one is liable
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The object did not move directly from רשות היחיד to רשות הרבים. It passed through a כרמלית, and there is no known source for liability in such a case.

steps.title: רב ספרא opens the answer in the name of רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: The answer to the challenge begins. רב ספרא quotes רבי אמי, who quotes רבי יוחנן. The content of the answer comes on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ספרא said in the name of רבי אמי, who said in the name of רבי יוחנן:
steps.whatsHappening: This line is a setup for the answer. It only gives the chain of names, and what רבי יוחנן actually said comes right on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא is about to defend the רבנן by showing a case where we do find this kind of liability. The answer is attributed through a chain of three אמוראים, all leading back to רבי יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who reports the teaching
An אמורא in ארץ ישראל and a student of רבי יוחנן

phrases.english: Rav Safra said
that Rabbi Ami said
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
phrases.notes: The content of his answer continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב סָפְרָא אָמַר רַבִּי אַמֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the answer to the challenge against the רבנן.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Precedent from a parallel case (content continues on the next amud)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought there was no precedent for liability when an object passes through a middle domain.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוחנן will show that such liability does exist (explained on the next amud).
